Article 235 does not take away an appeal right available under the law regulating an officer's service conditions. Article 235 does not authorise the High Court to deal with a judicial officer contrary to legally prescribed service conditions.
Article 236(a)'s district-judge definition includes a judge of a city civil court. Article 236(a) includes an assistant district judge. Article 236(a) includes the chief judge of a small cause court.

Article 236(a) includes an additional district judge. Article 236(a) includes a joint district judge. Article 236(a) includes the chief presidency magistrate. Article 236(a) includes an additional chief presidency magistrate.

In the broad district-court pattern, the same officer is district judge on the civil side and sessions judge on the criminal side. The district-level court in the supplied broad pattern has original as well as appellate jurisdiction, subject to the governing law. The district judge has judicial and administrative responsibilities and supervises subordinate courts in the district within the legal framework. District-level civil/criminal apex capacity (qualified general pattern).

In the supplied general civil hierarchy, subordinate judge corresponds to Civil Judge Senior Division/ClassI; nomenclature and jurisdiction remain State-specific. In the supplied general civil hierarchy, munsiff corresponds to Civil Judge Junior Division/ClassII; exact local nomenclature varies.

Small causes courts deal with specified small-value civil suits through a summary procedure under their applicable law. Some States have village-level panchayat courts for petty civil and criminal disputes; their existence and powers depend on the applicable State law.

Nyaya Panchayat, Gram Kutchery, Adalati Panchayat and Panchayat Adalat are names used in different States for local panchayat-court arrangements; they are not automatically identical to statutory Gram Nyayalayas.
The Forty-second Amendment Act,1976 expressly added the All India Judicial Service framework to Article 312.

Article 312(1) requires a Rajya Sabha national-interest resolution supported by at least two-thirds of members present and voting before Parliament may create an All India Service by law. The Article 312 resolution enables Parliament to create and regulate the All India Service by law; it does not itself constitute the service.
Article 312(4) permits necessary consequential changes to Part VI Chapter VI in an AIJS-creating law and says that law is not an Article 368 constitutional amendment.

Official parliamentary evidence identifies LawCommission report14(1958) among the AIJS recommendations. Official parliamentary evidence identifies LawCommission report77(1978) among the AIJS recommendations. Official parliamentary evidence identifies LawCommission report116(1986) among the AIJS recommendations.

Under BNSS 22(2), Sessions and Additional Sessions Judges may impose any sentence authorised by law, subject to High Court confirmation for death. A Sessions Court death sentence requires submission to and confirmation by the High Court; it cannot be executed without confirmation. High Court22(1) lawful-sentence power, expressly assessed in options.

Under the central BNSS 23(1) text, the CJM's sentencing power excludes imprisonment exceeding seven years. BNSS 23(1) excludes death and life imprisonment from a Chief Judicial Magistrate's sentencing power.

The central BNSS 23(2) general sentencing limit for a first-class magistrate is imprisonment up to three years. The central BNSS 23(2) general fine limit for a first-class magistrate is Rs 50,000, not the saved GBK325 Rs 5,000. The central BNSS 23(3) general imprisonment limit for a second-class magistrate is one year. The central BNSS 23(3) general fine limit for a second-class magistrate is Rs 10,000, not the saved GBK325 Rs 1,000.

BNSS 23(2),(3) include community service among the sentencing alternatives for both first- and second-class magistrates. The explanation to BNSS 23 describes community service as court-ordered punishment benefiting the community without remuneration to the convict.

BNSS 6 lists Courts of Session, first-class Judicial Magistrates, second-class Judicial Magistrates and Executive Magistrates besides High Courts and courts under other laws; metropolitan magistrates are not a separate class in this list.
